<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    Wildfires are increasing in frequency and severity due to climate change, becoming a major contributor to particulate matter air pollution (PM
                    <jats:sub>2.5</jats:sub>
                    ) in many regions of the globe. This study investigates whether daily exposure to wildfire-derived PM
                    <jats:sub>2.5</jats:sub>
                    increases violent assaults in Seattle, Washington, between 2013 and 2023. Using ground-level wildfire smoke presence as an instrument for PM
                    <jats:sub>2.5</jats:sub>
                    and crime report data from the Seattle Police Department, this study estimates a robust relationship between air pollution and urban violence. Over the study period, an average smoke-impacted day increased mean ambient PM
                    <jats:sub>2.5</jats:sub>
                    by 7.0
                    <jats:italic>μ</jats:italic>
                    g m
                    <jats:sup>−3</jats:sup>
                    , which corresponds to 3.6% more assaults. The findings contribute to the emerging literature linking environmental change to social tensions and demonstrate that climate-driven pollution may increase violence even in relatively low-pollution, high-capacity urban settings like Seattle. The study establishes the first direct estimate of a causal effect of wildfire smoke on assaults, leveraging eleven years of daily data and high-resolution smoke exposure data. As wildfires become a globally relevant source of pollution under future climate scenarios, these results underscore the societal benefits of climate change mitigation.
                  </jats:p>
title: Wildfire smoke increases assaults: evidence from Seattle
